You’ll find the equivalent in the game of dice where rolling a two or “snake eyes” means you've “crapped out.” So…. Americans developed this odd habit of tearing the corners off a two dollar “United States Note” (differentiated from a Federal Reserve Note by the Red seal) to neutralize the bad luck. …which meant $2’s wouldn't stay in circulation all that long due to consumer perpetrated mutilation. Question: Are prisoners getting an education in jail?
Old_Answer: Jails in the United States typically house inmates with charges awaiting trial and convicts serving less than a year. Realistically, there's not much demand for educational opportunities in the average municipal lockup. At the Salem/Roanoke County Jail where I was incarcerated, there WAS a walk-in library. We were fortunate in that regard, because many of the regional jails in our immediate vicinity (rural SW VA) had little more than a book storage closet and a trustee with a pushcart. There were no classes that I was made aware of. You could leave your cell and day room for rec/library time, visits to the commissary window, and prayer meeting. And that's about it. Ours was a work release pod so we DID get to put in a full eight hours five days a week. If we intended to learned anything while doing so, it was basically on us. Mostly, jail administration just wanted to see us serve our time and process out the other end. If we left jail an improved product, then nifty. But that was never the specific intent. The Big House is for learning. You wanna work on yourself then you better end up there. …because jail is a storage facility, not a community college.

Question: Do prisoners have any say in which other inmates they are friends with or are not friends with?
Old_Answer: Well…everybody has that choice, right? But jail is a microcosm. There was never more than twenty some men in the pod where I was incarcerated, so my potential choice of associates was limited. Of course, this was a couple of dozen bodies in a space that was meant to house less than half that many, so all interactions were up close and personal. There were inmates I associated with and those that I didn't, and while I understand racial tension is a given in larger prisons, it's not always as much of an issue in the smaller county facilities. My pod basically got along. I think the day after I was processed in, the place achieved a sort of ideal equilibrium that unfortunately was fleeting. My first cellmate, an alimony shirker and borderline abuser, got transferred up state, and I had a cell all my own for a blessed two nights. Prison is where a goodly portion of our lower class citizens get their post secondary school education. Students come and students go. Some matriculate in. Some transfer out. And some eventually graduate. I still keep in touch with one of the inmates I was housed with. I won't name him because he's managed to put his past behind him. And since he was never convicted of a felony, he's been largely successful in that effort. His is a place I'll never be.

Old_Answer: You know, I can understand how one might get the impression that specific behaviors are mandated in jail or prison due to prisoners adhering so meticulously to certain practices. But inmates have many self-imposed rules, and the sock thing is definitely one of these. Nobody in their right mind wants to put bare foot to floor in lockup. The only reasons I EVER removed my socks in county was — And that's it. Despite the CO’s wheeling in a janitorial cart once a day, and every con in the pod swabbing the day room floor, our individual cells (particularly the stainless steel toilet/sink combo), and the shower stall and additional open air communal head at the end of the second tier catwalk — despite all this — the surfaces in jail were never truly clean. Jails and prisons are veritable petri dishes for tinea pedis, protozoa, cold/flu viruses and your everyday run-of-the-mill despair. And in an environment where a relatively mundane illness can blossom into something life-threatening due to substandard healthcare, you do what you can to minimize contact. And if that means wearing socks and marginalizing bunkies who refuse to get with the program, then so be it. We called the few prisoners stupid enough to go barefoot in the pod “Jethros.” And it wasn't a term of endearment. Nobody wanted a Jethro for a cellmate. They usually ended up camping out on yoga mats under the corrugated steel stairway rather than getting a cellie. So the sock thing, like the courtesy flush, was a rule of our very own. And you broke it at your own peril.
